newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS-Waigel argues special case for Bonn on EMU.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Waigel argues special case for Bonn on EMU.

text.p: Germany argued forcefully on Tuesday that its growing debt mountain would not be a barrier to its qualification for European monetary union and that the single currency could go ahead -- with Germany -- in 1999.

Finance Minister Theo Waigel, bringing his European Union counterparts up to date on Bonn's plans to whip its economy into shape for monetary union, admitted that total debt would be above the target level set in the Maastricht Treaty.
But he argued that special factors were to blame for this and stressed Germany remained resolute in its bid to cut its running deficits to ensure they met the Maastricht target.
"We are making every effort to meet the criteria, and we will do so," Waigel told a briefing. "The criteria must be interpreted strictly."
He declined to be drawn on financial market speculation that Europe could delay the new currency's launch.

"At the moment everyone is making efforts to meet the criteria. We will decide who has done so next year on the basis of the actual figures for this year. This decision will not take place earlier or later than that time," Waigel said.
The Maastricht Treaty lays down economic targets on inflation, interest and exchange rates, budget deficits and public debt which nations must meet this year to join the euro.

The treaty calls for debt to total no more than 60 percent of gross domestic product -- or at least show significant progress in falling toward this level -- and for deficits to be three percent or less, except in exceptional circumstances.
Germany's economic convergence plan calls for a debt ratio of 61.5 percent to GDP this year. As the level is also rising, this does not meet the definition laid down in the Treaty.

Remaining insistent that the Maastricht criteria should not be softened, Waigel said special burdens such as German unification, the incorporation of debts from the German railways and transfers to eastern Europe nonetheless had to be taken into account in assessing Germany's debt burden.

"It is not the case that it is not allowed to point to such factors within a strict interpretation of the criteria," he said. There was no suggestion that he intended to apply the same special arguments to the German public deficit.
Earlier, a remark from Waigel to Germany's mass-circulation Bild newspaper had provoked renewed talk in financial markets that 1999 launch of the euro could be delayed.

Waigel, struggling to calm German fears that the planned euro will not be as stable as the mark, told Bild, "There won't be any soft euro with me. The important thing is: criteria have precedence over timetable."
"We shall in the next nine months do all we can to fulfil the Maastricht stability criteria."
Talk of a delay to the start of EMU was sparked by shock German unemployment data in January showing jobless queues at a post-war record.

Worries that Europe's former taskmaster could itself fail to qualify for EMU have centred on the deficit criteria, with economists judging Bonn's 2.9 percent deficit forecast as too optimistic and too close for comfort to the three percent goal.

While oppposition Social Democrat leader Oscar Lafontaine acknowledged on Monday that the government knew that it would not meet the deficit criteria for EMU, SPD budget spokesman Karl Diller, said Bonn did not stand a chance of meeting the criteria in time for the January 1, 1999 launch date because spending was "out of control."

Citing finance ministry data, Diller said the federal deficit for January and February already amounted to 34.8 billion marks ($20.6 billion), two thirds of the level of 53.3 billion budgeted for the full year.
"Chancellor (Helmut Kohl) should come clean on how things are to proceed with Europe. Under this government, Germany stands no chance of meeting the Maastricht goal," Diller said.

Waigel's comments came after his finance ministry at the weekend denied a report in news magazine Der Spiegel that internal government calculations showed the budget deficit climbing as high as 4.15 percent of GDP in 1997.

Separately, Gerhard Schroeder, premier of the state of Lower Saxony and tipped as SPD contender for the chancellorship in the 1998 general election, said EMU should be delayed as Germany could not qualify without creative accounting.
Schroeder told the Financial Times in an interview he did not believe a delay would damage Europe in the long run.

Meanwhile, German Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt said he was certain Germany would qualify on time. That view was echoed by the German Banking Federation which predicted a punctual EMU start. ($ = 1.690 German Marks)
